source.title: Limitations of refinement methods for weak to strong generalization
source.authors: Seamus Somerstep; Ya'acov Ritov; Mikhail Yurochkin; Subha Maity; Yuekai Sun

page_placements.theme: Theory refinements beyond 'must beat' (loss equivalence, bound tightness, limits under concept shift, boosting a weak generator)

record.file_problem: None noted; the text contains the paper and appendices through the Figure 1 details.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes and empirically compares weak training and refinement, reporting limitations and incomplete transfer. Its own results refine the scope of weak-to-strong methods, though it does not calculate PGR.
record.gate_note: Figure 1 reports weak-training, ICL-refinement, and oracle comparisons on GSM8K; the text says weak training does not successfully teach mathematical reasoning and refinement improves over weak training but remains below the oracle. Section 4.2 reports qualitative content/style outcomes for weak training and refinement on two persona tasks. The paper also proves inconsistency results under its latent-concept assumptions. Exact plotted scores are not stated in the text. The new identification procedure is omitted as a row because it is the authors’ alternative method, not weak-label training or refinement.
record.test_reason: The study replicates direct weak training (GPT-3.5-Turbo on GSM8K; GPT-4o-mini on persona tasks) and compares it with label refinement and an oracle. It also argues theoretically that both methods are inconsistent estimators under latent concept shift. Its results bear on V2, since refinement improves over naive weak training. V1 is touched, but the student-versus-supervisor comparison can only be read from plots.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that, under their latent concept transfer framework, both weak training and label refinement are biased and inconsistent, leaving a gap to an oracle. A deconvolution-style latent-concept identification procedure is consistent but idealized and impractical, which motivates more practical methods with good theoretical properties. Empirically, refinement beats weak training but stays below the oracle.
record.recipe_differences: Uses direct weak-label training and ICL label refinement, but evaluates them in the paper’s latent-concept framework and a toy persona-learning setting rather than reporting the original PGR measure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported qualitative outcomes differ between weak training and refinement and across GSM8K and the two persona-learning evaluations; the paper does not quantify task-specific PGR.

fits_no_version.finding: Under latent concept shift, weak training gives an inconsistent estimator, with error bounded below by source and weak-label biases (Prop. 3.1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weak training on biased weak labels plus source data cannot consistently recover the target function under latent concept shift.

fits_no_version.finding: Refinement retains irreducible bias when inferred latent-concept proportions are wrong. Empirically, the persona is not fully transferred (style scores).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label refinement leaves a gap to the oracle or target because it misweights latent concepts.

record.problems: The empirical comparisons are reported qualitatively or in plots without exact scores, PGR, or stated uncertainty. The persona experiment is described as a toy empirical setting, and the theoretical conclusions depend on the paper's latent-concept assumptions.
record.rows_left_out: The oracle and latent-concept identification results are discussed in the text and shown in Figure 1 or Figure 3, but are alternative methods rather than weak-label training/refinement results to catalogue here. No other qualifying results were left out.

untested.parts: PGR, and whether the student exceeds weak-supervisor accuracy. Figure 1 and Figure 3 plot these quantities, but the text gives no numbers.
Auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling weak supervisors, and loss variants. PGR is not computed, so only the direction of refinement's gain is shown.
Size sweeps, chess, reward modelling, and predictors of PGR.
Exploitation of what the supervisor can't check, distribution shift, and shared errors.
Conditions under which the student must beat its supervisor. The theory addresses consistency toward the target instead.

missing.what: Numeric weak-model accuracy vs GPT-3.5-Turbo accuracy under weak training, refinement and the oracle (x-axis weak accuracy roughly 0.04–0.14). These values are needed to compute PGR for V1 and V2.
Weak-model vs strong-model content and style scores per weak supervisor (x-axis weak score, y-axis strong score). These would settle whether the student beats its supervisor.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The study's own empirical results are qualitative statements about plots, with no PGR and no uncertainty. For R1, the statement that GPT-3.5 'does not successfully learn any mathematical reasoning ability' from weak labels hints at a V1 failure on GSM8K. It does not state performance relative to the weak supervisor, so no V1 verdict is given. The study is COLM 2025.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not report PGR or provide exact comparisons establishing whether each student beats its weak supervisor; the plotted values are not stated numerically.
Auxiliary confidence losses, ensembling weak supervisors, and loss variants are not tested.
No PGR sweep by supervisor or student size, representations, chess, or reward modelling. The paper reports qualitative results on GSM8K and persona-learning tasks, not task-specific PGR.
The paper does not test supervisor-uncheckable exploits, PGR changes under distribution shift, or effects of shared errors.
The theoretical results concern estimator consistency and bias, not conditions under which a student must outperform its supervisor.
